Messages.Author: John P.
Messages.Body:
Adequate card stock (survives the bend test)

The premature wear on the edges sucks.

Players loved the solid booster packs rather than
some of the very thin wrappers that past sets have featured.

Can anyone help me with why the starter decks are split
into two sealed sections. It appeared that all the rares and
vampires were in one "section" so I cannot imagine that it
is for demo or teaching purposes.

The draft effects are coolness

The cards themselves are interesting.

Why bother with uncommons? Why not just
print all vampires as uncommon, have a rare slot,
and everything else is common. It would make sooo
much sense.
New players get the card they need, older
players get decent amounts of the new stuff.
Maybe the odd uncommon like Black hand did
but nothing new... just reprints where we do not need
to see whole bunches of the cards.

And why the frell are there no references to the imbued
in the rulebook? We have trophy and redlist in the rules,
but I stll have to haul around 5 rules cards to figure out
those freakish imbued. I do not even think that the imbued
appear in the glossary or even get a mention in the rule book.
This of course led to hopeful speculation at the pre-release that the
imbued would like to be forgotten by White Wolf or perhaps our
wildest dreams would come true and they would be banned.
Since the next set is rumored (confirmed?) to be a sixty card
set there will be no starters and no imbued rules in their either.
Sad.

-John P.
Winnipeg

There are no uncommons.... only 110 R2s.
Begin painful math....

Given:

Each 3rd Ed. booster contains 11 cards
5 commons, 2 uncommons, 3 vamp, 1 Rare

There are 100 different commons in boosters, all of which appear to be
reprints

There are 100 different uncommons in boosters

There would seem to be 100 different vampires in the boosters. (I'm
uncertain exactly how many of the 124 vampires are starter only,
excluding the reprinted vamps but I suspect 100 is the number.)

There are 90 different rares, 80 R1 and 10 R2.

------------------
We get 5 commons per booster
36 boosters a box
100 commons to select from

5 * 36 / 100 = 1.8 of each common in one box

------------------
We get 2 uncommons per booster
36 boosters
100 uncommond to select from

2 * 36 / 100 = 0.72 of each uncommon in one box or one and a half boxes
for a complete set of uncommons (on average)

------------------
Similarly for vampires:
3*36/100 = 1.08 of each vampire in one box
------------------
Rares:
36 Rares in a box
80% of those rares are R1.
36 * 0.80 = 28.8 R1s / 80 R1s total = 0.36 of each R1 per box or a
complete set of R1s in three boxes.

20% of those rares are R2.
36 * .20 = 7.2 R2s / 10 R2s total = 0.72 of each R2 per box
(one and a half boxes to get a full set)
----------------------

Now if you have been paying attention you will notice that what white
wolf has done here is made uncommons the same rarity as R2s.

So you buy a box of 36 boosters and you expect to get
0.72 of each uncommon and 0.72 of each R2.

The theory of rarities with respect to VTES has always seemed to be
that the rares are cards you do not need a whole bunch of (eg: Praxis
seizures, Crusades) although there have been exceptions (eg War
Ghouls). By cramming uncommons into boosters in addition to the vampire
slots (where a few uncommons used to reside) and having so many
uncommons in a set, they have elevated uncommons to R2s.

So while my initial post said to do away with uncommons and put them in
the common slot, your response was that we needed uncommons. What has
actually happened though is that there is no uncommons, just 110 R2s in
the set with 3 R2s and either another R2 or an R1 in the booster.

I would rather see a proliferation of the new cards than have a hard
time finding them.

Now if White Wolf had decided to print 7 commons in each booster (7c 3v
1R) and made the existing commons into C2s the following occurs:
C2: 1.68 copies per box (you get 12 less of the reprinted commons in a
single box)
c1: 0.84 copies per booster (you get 12 more uncommons which includes
new cards per box of boosters)
and the R2s are actually slightly more rare than C2s.

If we made the reprinted commons cards C3 and the "uncommons" C2 you
would get 1.5 of each reprinted common in a box and 1.0 of each common.

Are more "uncommons" per box and less "commons" that important? While
they are to me, and anybody trying to make Tupdog decks or Mexico City
circle blood brothers probably thinks so cause this jerking around the
rarities is what made them difficult to get in sufficient numbers.

Well I've done more math here than I like to do in several years.
Ignore it as you please.

Call a common a common, an uncommon an uncommon. Uncommons need to be
more plentiful than rares and commons must be more plentiful than both.
Either cut down the number of uncommons in a set or deal with it in
some other manner please.

-John P.
Winnipeg

Of course there are uncommons. The cards in the uncommon slots are
uncommons. The point that their commonality is exactly equal to an
R2 is interesting on some rarity-geek level but it really doesn't
alter the fact. It does illuminate the point that you should never
try to understand rarity from just the textual, subjective description
of the rarity level (that is, "rare", "uncommon", or "common") alone.
Accurate information includes all the factors: number of slots in
the pack, instances printed on the card sheet, total number of cards
on the card, and price of the pack. I just take all this as
understood by anyone who wants to discuss.

> I would rather see a proliferation of the new cards than have a hard
> time finding them.

I'm not sure what this statement means. "Proliferation" is a poor
choice of words, I think, to convey your meaning. Do you mean that
you want to see lots of different new cards designed and printed? Or
that you want to see the new cards that _have_ been designed and
printed get into the hands of more people? Or possibly something
else?

> Now if White Wolf had decided to print 7 commons in each booster (7c 3v
> 1R) and made the existing commons into C2s the following occurs:
> C2: 1.68 copies per box (you get 12 less of the reprinted commons in a

> c1: 0.84 copies per booster (you get 12 more uncommons which includes
> new cards per box of boosters)
> and the R2s are actually slightly more rare than C2s.
>
> If we made the reprinted commons cards C3 and the "uncommons" C2 you
> would get 1.5 of each reprinted common in a box and 1.0 of each common.

I'm not sure what you're getting at. All of a sudden, you're changing the
subject from "Should there be an uncommon rarity level?" to a question of
the commonality of reprinted vs. new cards. The one has nothing to do with
the other. Perhaps you're unaware that under the system used in Third
Edition, the new cards are spread out over all rarity levels in almost
equal numbers, not counting the vampires: 12 rare (1 R2 rare, I believe),
12 uncommon, and 12 common. Furthermore, that goal really has nothing
to do with the use of an uncommon rarity level - you could pursue it or
ignore it equally well with or without an uncommon level, though some
of the specific means of doing so would change.

And yet furthermore, the goal of increasing the overall commonality of
new cards is not a universally shared one. Your first post suggested
that this is an obvious goal ("...make so much sense.") but it really
is not. Third Edition is supposed to be a base set. This is a goal
that is to a fair degree diametrically opposed to the notion of filling
it with new expansion cards. In fact, for player purposes, the best
choice would be to have no new cards in Third Edition at all - leaving
to the individual players whether they needed reprinted cards or not.
If they don't, they can just ignore the set altogether. The problem
comes when you print a few new cards amongst a card population of
that's predominantly reprints, since both newer and older players need
the new cards but only the newer players need the reprints in great
number. Unfortunately, White Wolf wants to see Third Edition to older
players as well so they're "salting" it with enough new cards -
including the vampires - to put us over a barrel without really
interfering with the goal of including enough well-tested staple
cards to make it usable as a base set.

> Are more "uncommons" per box and less "commons" that important?

No.

> While
> they are to me, and anybody trying to make Tupdog decks or Mexico City
> circle blood brothers probably thinks so cause this jerking around the
> rarities is what made them difficult to get in sufficient numbers.

I don't have the slightest idea what you're talking about. Common
vampires in an all-new-card expansion is yet a totally different
subject once again..

> Call a common a common, an uncommon an uncommon.

We are.

> Uncommons need to be more plentiful than rares

They are - they just aren't more plentiful than R2s. When you
bring instance numbers into the discussion, you confuse the
definition of "rare", "uncommon", and "common" - which are terms that
don't accurately describe precise rarity levels and never have - even
more than it already is. And, as far as I can see, the above
statement has no merit. Uncommons don't really need to be more
plentiful than rare (twos). They just need to be an intuitive
identifier of the relative number of slots in a pack.

> and commons must be more plentiful than both.
> Either cut down the number of uncommons in a set or deal with it in
> some other manner please.

I still have no idea what it is that bothers you about them. I see
no problem whatsoever with the rarity scheme in this sense. I would rather
see whole editions of cards be either all reprints or all new cards.
From a player perspective, _that_ makes sense. But I suspect it has
little chance to happen as long as White Wolf perceives they can make
more money overall by salting a base set with a few new cards.

Fred

>>> Fred Scott wrote:
>>>> Eh? What about cards that are less useful in large
>>>> numbers than common cards but more useful in larger
>>>> numbers than rare cards?
>
> I would rather have more cards than I can use than
> not enough cards to use effectively. I can give away
> extra cards. I cannot use or give away what I do not have.

You're still losing me. Uncommon vs. rare vs. common
cards are an orthogonal issue to this one. All you're
saying is, "Please add more cards that I can use effectively
and less of the ones I can't." Rarity levels only matter
in relationship to the usefulness of the card in whatever
numbers it's useful in. Wake with Evening's Freshness
isn't common enough as a common; Carver's Meat Packing and
Storage may be too common as a rare - but is still useful
in the right deck and metagame. It all just depends.

>>>> I don't understand the question. The usefulness
>>>> of having an uncommon ratio is obvious.
>
> Not obvious to me to me if it means having an uncommon
> slot means I will have difficulty getting the quantity
> of each card I feel I need. A narrow point of view perhaps.

Nope. You're just looking at the wrong complaint to express
what I think (as best I can tell from what you write) is
your issue. I'm completely confused why you've focused in
on a particular rarity level as the problem. But since
each card is needed at some different level and as they
vary all over the map, clearly, if you want a quantity
of each card you feel you need, it is necessary that
at least _some_ of the cards come in at the uncommon
rarity level. It is the correct level for some of
them.

>> Sure. All rarity levels can be likewise be compared to other
>> rarity levels by multiplying the relative instance indicator.
>> You find this profound?
>
> I never claimed it was profound. This is a newsgroup afterall.
> If everything on this group has to be profound it will get real quiet
> in here real quick.

"Profound" means interesting and meaningful to some end
conclusion that isn't already obvious to everybody. U1s = R2s
in an expansion that comes in packs with two slots of uncommons
to one slot of rares is an obvious thing and, as far as I can see,
a rather meaningless point. If you're not getting as many of some
particular card as you would want in an expansion, the answer is
to increase its overall rarity, whatever that is. Whether it's
C1, U1, R2 or R1, none of that matters. It's just a question of
making it bigger than whatever level it's at.

>> Of course there are uncommons. The cards in the uncommon slots are
>> uncommons. The point that their commonality is exactly equal to an
>> R2 is interesting on some rarity-geek level but it really doesn't
>> alter the fact. It does illuminate the point that you should never
>> try to understand rarity from just the textual, subjective description
>> of the rarity level (that is, "rare", "uncommon", or "common") alone.
>> Accurate information includes all the factors: number of slots in
>> the pack, instances printed on the card sheet, total number of cards
>> on the card, and price of the pack. I just take all this as
>> understood by anyone who wants to discuss.
>
> I find that a very big assumption on your part that your average card player works out the math.

Well, people don't actually have to work out the math, I suppose.
If you're going to make an argument about it, it helps to know
whether your individual experience with a card's rarity was typical
or atypical. Anyway, the point is, I don't see what problem is
caused by the fact that the commonality of U1s exactly equals that
of an R2s.

> Then let me rephrase, "I would rather see an abundance of the new cards in a
> set than a difficult time finding them among the reprints" ie more quantity of each new card per box than the current
> distribution.

OK, got it.

>> Furthermore, that goal really has nothing
>> to do with the use of an uncommon rarity level - you could pursue it or
>> ignore it equally well with or without an uncommon level, though some
>> of the specific means of doing so would change.
>
> While my premise in the original post was the elimination of uncommons
> my envisioned goal of this was getting more of the new cards. That is how the two relate.

But that isn't a relationship. As I said, the one has nothing to do with
the other. Increasing a card's frequency, whether new or old, has to do
with increasing whatever it is. A C1 would have to be increased to a C2
or something higher. A U1's frequency could be increased by making it
a C1, it's true. But you could also do it by making it U2. The new
R1 cards could be increased by making them U1s. Eliminating "uncommon",
as an entire rarity level, wouldn't seem to have anything to do with any
of this. That just removes an option from the table. How does that
help?

> I missed the equal spread of new cards among the three rarities. It has been

> pointed out. While it does alter the argument, it does not change the

> fact that the frequency of an uncommon's appearance is decreasing.

"The frequency of an uncommon's appearance is decreasing." I don't understand
that sentence. Decreasing in comparison to what?

> Is the goal to get new players the cards they need in the quantity they
> need or to give them just one of each card (at best) per box so they can
> say, "geeze, wish I had more of these".

Well, of course, not being an employee, I can't give you the real answer
to that. I would speculate that if they feel if they put too many new
library cards in the mix, Third Edition would make a poor base set. A base
set is supposed to be comprised of staple cards of well-known quality so
beginning players can buy it to form the basis of their collections. If
you were a new player, you'd be poorly served by several boxes of, say,
Gehenna boosters to start your collection. You need cards like Govern
the Unaligned and Lost in Crowds and Freak Drive. You don't want to
start with lots of copies of Chain of Command. I suspect it would be very
risky to create a ton of new library cards from scratch and throw them
together and call them a base set. Too many of them would miss the mark.

>> And yet furthermore, the goal of increasing the overall commonality of
>> new cards is not a universally shared one. Your first post suggested
>> that this is an obvious goal ("...make so much sense.") but it really
>> is not. Third Edition is supposed to be a base set. This is a goal
>> that is to a fair degree diametrically opposed to the notion of filling
>> it with new expansion cards.
>
> I did not ask for it to be filled with new cards, I just want to be able to a subjectively reasonale number of each of the new
> cards and still be able
> to pay the rent.

Understood. So would I and, I think, a number of other players who already
have established card collections. Unfortunately, to fulfill its purpose,
this set needs to contain an overwhelming number of reprint library cards.
And to have an overwhelming number of reprint library cards, logically
it has to have few new cards.

> A new player doesn't care about if the card is new or reprinted.

Yes and no. He may not exactly care if the cards he's buying has
been printed in a previous set. But he cares about the quality of
the card. And the most flexible and useful cards in the game, the ones
easiest to build basic, effective decks from are necessarily reprints.
New cards in expansions full of new cards tend to concentrate on
specialized themes, much more useful to players who already own a
solid base collection of cards.

> They just want the card based soley on its own merits. Now I assume
> you are talking about a player who has played for a while but does not
> have cards from camarilla edition [last base set] and earlier (not
> exactly a new player).

I'm not sure what hair you're splitting. I'm dividing my populations
of players between players who have enough staple cards and those who
don't. The former want new cards; the latter need an expansion with
a high degree of standard, salt-of-earth, reliable staple cards.

> Due to the size of the set and having four different rarity sheets
> this player will have difficulty getting the reprints in sufficient
> quantity to build a reliable deck, just as the new player will have
> difficulty getting quanties of the new cards. This large a set caters
> to players buying large quantities. That is usually not a new player.

It sort of has to be. That is, new players who want to build reliable
decks have to invest at a certain level or they're just not going to
be able to get enough stock. Agreed, the size of the set works against
people who don't want to spend a lot of money. But since even the
basic Jyhad game contains a wide latitude of strategies, different
clans and disciplines, etc., the base set has to be large. All base
sets in this game have been this large. There's no way to get around
it.

There are ways for people who don't want to spend so much money to
still make good decks, though. Precon decks will allow the players
to build up a fairly large number of good clan or discipline-specific
staple cards without spending much money. Trading cards is the other
poor man's friend - buy packs and put the cards that are not in his area
of interest up for trade in exchange for those that are.

> I guess it really relates to the size of the set. Because the set is 290 cards plus vampires the amount required to buy to get a
> desired quantity
> is higher than smaller sets.

Agreed. The alternative would be to make even more specialized base
sets. We already have Camarilla Edition for Camarilla clans and
Third Edition for the Sabbat. I suppose you could divide the two base
sets into four and halve the number of clans covered by each, thus
mitigating the problem. For a number of reasons, I don't think White
Wolf would find that route very palatable, though. In any case, this
is a far cry from saying, "Uncommon rarity level is bad."

> Reprints don't bother me. I can always use more base cards
> as I can build/give decks to new players. But I do not
> even get enough of each reprint to build a deck for a new
> player with say 6 carrion crows unless I buy about three boxes.

Then this is a complaint that is entirely about set size. If they
printed 50 rares, 50 uncommons, and 50 commons, your problem would
be lessened. This is a different argument.

>>> While
>>> they are to me, and anybody trying to make Tupdog decks or Mexico City
>>> circle blood brothers probably thinks so cause this jerking around the
>>> rarities is what made them difficult to get in sufficient numbers.
>>
>> I don't have the slightest idea what you're talking about. Common
>> vampires in an all-new-card expansion is yet a totally different
>> subject once again..
>
> I apologize that you do not see the connection between the most
> recent issue with getting sufficient quantities of a card that screamed
> "play with lots of these cards in your deck" and the situation
> now where getting sufficient quantities of a specific card is difficult.

I'm beginning to. If set size is your issue, this relates to common
vampires not being common enough. The complaints you've articulated
do not. You want set sizes to be smaller so you can get more of a
given card in a box of a particular set. That makes sense - and was
a complaint that many had about Legacies of Blood, by the way.

>>> Uncommons need to be more plentiful than rares
>>
>> They are - they just aren't more plentiful than R2s.

..

> The we are just going to disagree here. I believe the average
> player expects more uncommons than rares, whatever the
> numbers on the checklist that they have never seen means.

I don't think they do, no. I believe, I hope, that most people
understand that how U1s and R2s relate to each other is ultimately
unimportant. I still am not quite sure what your issue with it is.
I think you've somehow conflated it with the causes of some of the
other things you've complained about. Getting enough of a given
card in a box of cards so that you can get a playable collection
from an affordable number of boxes purchased has nothing to do
with U1 vs. R2 commonality. It has to do with set size and
setting appropriate overall rarity levels for each particular
card.

Fred

Um, I don't see the point of equating Legacies of Blood vampires
to uncommons. LoB has vampires, 3E has vampires. LoB had
uncommon cards (well, two to be exact), 3E has uncommon cards.
Of course, the nature of the cards listed as "uncommon" differs
entirely from LoB to 3E. In the former case, two cards were listed
as uncommons and they were spread in an artificially low freqency
amongst some of the common cards. In the latter case, there were
actual card slots and 100 U1 cards.

Also note that although three slots out of eleven were allocated
to vampires in Legacies of Blood and in Third Edition, they
were divide amongst 50 vampires in LoB vs. 100 in Third Edition.
So vampires were essentially "V2s" in Legacies of Blood, if you
want to compare apples to apples.

Different sets, completely different rarity situation. I'm
completely confused what's even the point of comparing the
two. And I'm even more confused what is the point of comparing
the two while conflating "vampires" in the one with "uncommon
library cards" in the other. Again, I think your issue is set
size, not the existance of an uncommon rarity level.

By the way, just for yuks, I'll throw in my observation about
the common rarity level in Legacies of Blood. Seven card
slots were advertised as containing "common" cards. But, in
fact, I believe the first two contained one set of common
cards, the other five contained a different set. And the
members of the first group seemed to be on a cardsheet that
numbered 45 cards vs. an 80-card cardsheet for the other -
meaning that the "common" rarity levels were slightly different.
Cards in the first group appeared twice in every 45 packs (or
once in every 22 and 1/2 packs) vs. one time in every 16 packs
for the second group. I believe the first group was reprints
and the second group was new common cards.

>>> Is the goal to get new players the cards they need in the quantity they
>>> need or to give them just one of each card (at best) per box so they can
>>> say, "geeze, wish I had more of these".
>>
>> Well, of course, not being an employee, I can't give you the real answer
>> to that. I would speculate that if they feel if they put too many new
>> library cards in the mix, Third Edition would make a poor base set.
>
> My line above was regardless of new or reprint (as both have the same frequency).
> A new player looking for aid from bats will likely only get two from a box.
> That is hardly enough for a staple card. For uncommons it is one per
> box. Hope a new player does not need more than 1 freak drive.

Sure. That's a function of set size.

But presumedly, a new player needs more Aid From Bats than Freak Drives.
If not, then the issue is that Freak Drive, specifically, should be more
common no matter how large the set. In the case of Freak Drive, that's
arguable - but only because Freak Drive is so useful that it's even suspiciously
underprinted at the uncommon level. Most uncommon cards do not prompt the
same suspicion.

> Same applies to cool new cards.
>
>>> A new player doesn't care about if the card is new or reprinted.
>>
>> Yes and no. He may not exactly care if the cards he's buying has
>> been printed in a previous set. But he cares about the quality of
>> the card. And the most flexible and useful cards in the game, the ones
>> easiest to build basic, effective decks from are necessarily reprints.
>> New cards in expansions full of new cards tend to concentrate on
>> specialized themes, much more useful to players who already own a
>> solid base collection of cards.
>
> I disagree here. You are claiming that nothing in a new set could
> become a staple card?

I didn't say that. A few could very well be new staple card. On the
Que Vive certainly appears to be one. But it's hard to design large
numbers of new staple cards for a number of reasons. Therefore, a
base set is composed of overwhelming numbers of reprints.

> I still maintain that a brand-new player does not care if a card
> is new or reprinted. As long as it is good. A new card has the
> potential to be good.

I disagree. The sentence, "A new card has the potential to be good"
is so ambiguous as to serve any purpose in that a line of logic.
It is not "profound". :-P

New players specifically need flexible, useful cards. And - though
new cards do indeed have the "potential to be good" - quite honestly
the average new card tends not to be that good. That may shock you
but if you think about it, it's absolutely true. If you think of
the card most people tend to use most, they're many of them original
Jyhad cards that were first printed in 1994. Maybe not a majority
any more; there's so many other cards that have been created since
thing. But, in relatition to the raw numbers, I'm sure original
Jyhad cards (or reprints thereof) are used in tournament winning
decks in ratios vastly out of proportion to their ratio in the
overall card population. There's a reason for this: the character
of the original game uses them as its backbone in them. And,
although the game has evolved over time due to the new cards printed
ever so often, there would be a player revolt if it were to be
utterly changed in a single expansion. In order to avoid that,
I believe the designers are rather cautious about designing new
cards; many of them just aren't very good. A relative handful
are reasonable. And a few are truly stellar and become favorites.
Those favorites crack the "staple card" club and some of them have
been reprinted in Third Edition.

If the designers where to create a new base set out of newly designed
cards, they couldn't possibly be as conservative as they are about the
average card utility when designing the usual all-new sets. If they
were, they would fail and the new set would never be looked on as
a useful base set. If they weren't, they'd make mistakes from time
to time (designing so many powerful cards in a single set) and
likely design an over-the-top card that would soon have to get banned
or given errata. Banning or issuing errata to overpowered cards is a
bad thing. So a successful base set really needs to be reprints.
Or, at the very least, it would require a lot more playtesting time
than White Wolf seems willing to spend. So reprints it is.

Fred

I've seen the same complaint in the local mailing lists down here
(which makes the complaint seem even stupid, since the set didn't even
made the country yet and all we've seen of the draft text was a single
card preview). My usual response is: how different it is from the
outferior on cards that require a bloodline-specific discipline? Or,
going further, how much difficult it is to ignore draft text than it is
to ignore, say, the [dom] text on Spirit Marionette when you're using
it at [OBE]?

Messages.Author: Fred Scott

"Fabio 'Sooner' Macedo" <fabio....@gmail.com> wrote in message news:1157984583.3...@p79g2000cwp.googlegroups.com...

> So, for what you guys are saying, it is even *easier* to ignore draft
> text than it is to ignore outferior text, something we've been doing
> since Bloodlines was released. :P

Eh? Does anyone down there use Nose of the Hound? How about Clotho's
Gift. Those two cards, at least, I've seen more in decks that use them
for their outferior and don't even pack any vampires possessing their
main Bloodline Discipline than I've seen them played in decks that do.
The reason is that their outferiors are useful enough that the huge
difference in the popularity of the outferier discipline in comparison
to that of the Bloodline discipline (that is for instance, many vampires
have auspex, only a few possess Spiritus) comes into play.

There may be other examples. These two are the ones that come quickest
to my mind.

> (barring specific cases where the bloodline discipline uses "as [disc]
> above" referencing to the outferior, of course).

Actually, I can't think of any reason what that would make a difference.
It's true Nose of the Hound is worded that way - but so is Tangle Atropos'
Hand and the potence version of TAH doesn't particularly impress me. On
the other hand, the obfuscate version of Clotho's Gift (by contrast) does.

Fred
